Section 1 of 14

Could simply looking at something save a dying person?

The story sounds strange.

People were dying from poisonous snakebites. The Creator told Moses to make a bronze serpent, lift it on a pole, and invite the people to look at it.

Those who looked lived.

There was no medicine in the bronze. The object had no magical power. Healing came from the Creator, but each person had to decide whether to trust His instructions.

Centuries later, Jesus said this story pointed directly to Him.

Trouble in the wilderness

Read Numbers 21:4–9 ↗.

The people of Israel had been freed from slavery, but their journey through the wilderness was difficult. They became discouraged and spoke against the Creator and Moses.

They complained about the food the Creator had provided and questioned why He had led them out of Egypt.

Their words revealed something deeper than frustration. They were rejecting the One who had rescued, protected, and fed them.

Poisonous snakes entered the camp, and many people were bitten.

The desert already contained dangers. The Creator had been protecting His people as they traveled. When they repeatedly rejected Him, He allowed them to experience what life was like without the protection they had taken for granted.

Their rebellion had consequences.

The people admitted their wrong

Read Numbers 21:7 ↗.

The people came to Moses and said:

“We have sinned.”

They stopped blaming the journey, the wilderness, Moses, and the Creator. They told the truth about their own choices.

That was the beginning of healing.

We often want relief without repentance. We want the Creator to remove the consequences while we continue protecting the choices that caused them.

Repentance means more than feeling afraid of consequences. It means admitting what is wrong and turning back toward the Creator.

The Creator provided one remedy

The Creator told Moses to make a bronze serpent and place it on a pole. Anyone who had been bitten could look at it and live.

Imagine two people lying in the same camp. Both have been bitten. Both are dying. Both hear that the Creator has provided a remedy.

One person says:

“That makes no sense. Looking at a bronze serpent cannot heal me.”

The other says:

“I do not understand it, but I trust the Creator.”

One refuses to look. The other turns toward the pole and lives.

The difference was not intelligence, family background, social position, or personal goodness.

The difference was trust.

The bronze serpent had no power of its own

The people were not told to pray to the bronze serpent, carry it as a charm, or treat it as a spiritual being.

It was a temporary symbol pointing beyond itself to the Creator’s saving power.

Years later, people began burning incense to that same bronze serpent. They turned a God-given symbol into an object of worship.

Read 2 Kings 18:1–4 ↗.

King Hezekiah destroyed it and called it “Nehushtan,” meaning simply a piece of bronze.

This teaches an important lesson: even a symbol that once carried a helpful message can become spiritually dangerous when people give the object power that belongs only to the Creator.

An object, image, symbol, place, or religious item cannot forgive sin or save a life. We should understand what symbols mean, evaluate them by Scripture, and worship the Creator rather than the things He made.

Jesus explained the symbol

Read John 3:14–17 ↗.

Jesus said:

“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

The bronze serpent pictured the deadly problem. Jesus carried that problem to the cross.

Read 2 Corinthians 5:21 ↗ and 1 Peter 2:24 ↗.

Jesus never sinned, but He took our sins upon Himself. He carried our guilt and accepted the death sin produces.

The serpent on the pole pointed forward to Jesus lifted on the cross.

The Israelites looked and received physical life. We look to Jesus in faith and receive eternal life.

The poison of sin has reached everyone

Read Romans 3:23 ↗ and Romans 6:23 ↗.

Every person has been wounded by sin.

Sin appears in different forms:

  • Pride
  • Hatred
  • Dishonesty
  • Sexual wrongdoing
  • Greed
  • Addiction
  • Jealousy
  • Violence
  • Unforgiveness
  • Religious hypocrisy
  • Refusing the Creator’s authority

We may compare ourselves with other people and decide that our sins are not as serious as theirs. But a person dying from poison does not become healthy by finding someone who is closer to death.

Every one of us needs the same Savior.

Sin is not merely breaking a religious rule. It damages trust, separates us from the Creator, harms other people, and leads toward death.

We cannot remove that poison by our own goodness.

The cross may carry painful memories

For many Native people, the cross has not always been presented as a sign of love.

Crosses appeared in institutions connected with forced religious instruction, boarding schools, cultural shame, and family separation. People who carried the name of Jesus sometimes acted in ways completely opposed to Him.

That history can make it difficult to see the cross without also seeing abuse.

Those feelings should not be dismissed.

But the cross did not begin as a symbol of institutional power. It was an instrument the Roman government used to shame, torture, and execute people.

At the cross, Jesus was not the colonizer. He was the innocent One suffering under political violence, religious corruption, false accusations, and public humiliation.

He willingly entered human pain and allowed powerful people to wound Him. Then He transformed an instrument of death into the place where sin was defeated.

People have misused His name, but their actions do not change what Jesus did.

He did not die to turn Native people into Europeans. He died to reconcile people from every nation to their Creator.

The Father did not force Jesus to die

Read John 10:17–18 ↗ and 2 Corinthians 5:18–19 ↗.

Jesus willingly gave His life.

The Father and Son were not working against one another. The Creator was acting through Jesus to reconcile the world to Himself.

The cross shows both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love.

Justice could not pretend evil did not matter. Love would not abandon us to its result. Jesus took our place and opened a path home.

What does it mean to look to Jesus?

Looking to Jesus does not mean staring at a picture or wearing a cross.

It means turning your trust toward Him.

Admit that you have been wounded by sin

Stop pretending that you can heal yourself. Tell the truth about what you have done and what sin has done to you.

Believe that Jesus is enough

Read Acts 4:12 ↗.

You do not need another spiritual mediator, secret ceremony, or payment. Jesus is fully able to save you.

Receive His forgiveness

Read 1 John 1:9 ↗.

Confess your sins and accept His promise to forgive and cleanse you.

Turn from the old direction

Faith is more than agreeing with information about Jesus. It includes repentance—a willingness to leave the path that is destroying you.

Follow Him

Keep looking to Jesus through prayer, Scripture, obedience, and daily dependence on the Holy Spirit.

The first look brings life. Continuing to look keeps your heart connected to the One who gave it.

Salvation is a gift, not a complicated test

Read Ephesians 2:8–9 ↗.

The dying Israelites did not earn healing.

They were not told to complete a long ceremony, pay Moses, prove that they deserved help, or understand exactly how the miracle worked.

They were told to look.

In the same way, you cannot purchase salvation, inherit it from your family, or earn it through good behavior.

You receive it by trusting Jesus.

Good works follow salvation, but they do not buy it. Obedience is the life that grows after you have looked to Jesus and received His grace.

What if you do not feel forgiven?

Feelings can change from one hour to the next.

You may confess your sin and still feel ashamed. You may remember what happened and wonder whether the Creator could truly accept you.

Do not make your feelings the judge of His promise.

Read John 6:37 ↗.

Jesus said:

“The one who comes to Me I will by no means cast out.”

Your confidence rests in His character, not in the strength of your emotions.

The Israelites were not healed because they felt the right feeling. They were healed because they trusted the Creator enough to look.

Faith says:

“I still feel the wound, but I trust the One who promised life.”

Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence

A person healed from the snakebite still remembered being bitten.

In the same way, forgiveness restores your relationship with the Creator, but some earthly consequences may remain.

You may need to:

  • Apologize
  • Return something you took
  • Rebuild trust over time
  • Accept legal consequences
  • Seek treatment
  • Repair financial damage
  • Maintain new boundaries
  • Change relationships or routines

Making things right does not purchase forgiveness. It demonstrates that repentance is becoming real in your life.

Jesus removes condemnation and then teaches you how to walk differently.

What if you look away again?

Read Hebrews 3:12–14 ↗ and John 15:4–5 ↗.

Jesus does not abandon you every time you struggle. But He will not force you to remain connected to Him.

A person can choose to turn away, resist the Holy Spirit, and return to a life of unbelief.

That is why the Bible tells us to continue in faith.

Do not depend on one emotional experience from years ago. Remain with Jesus today.

If you fall, look toward Him again. Confess what happened, receive His forgiveness, and stand back up.

The answer to failure is not hiding from Jesus. It is returning to Him.

Do not stare only at the wound

When someone has been bitten, examining the wound will not remove the poison.

Some people spend their lives looking only at their failures:

“I ruined everything.”
“I should have known better.”
“I will always be this way.”
“No one could forgive what I did.”

Honest self-examination is important, but shame becomes another trap when it keeps your attention away from Jesus.

You are not saved by thinking about your sin more intensely. You are saved by looking to the Savior.

Your wound may explain why you need help. It does not have the authority to decide your future.

Point people toward Jesus without forcing them

Moses lifted the bronze serpent where people could see it. He could not force anyone to look.

Our calling is similar.

We can explain who Jesus is, show what He has done, answer questions, and live in a way that reflects His love. But we must not use fear, pressure, political power, or cultural erasure to force a decision.

Forced religion contradicts the invitation of Jesus.

Read John 12:32 ↗.

Jesus said that when He was lifted up, He would draw people to Himself.

Our responsibility is to lift up Jesus clearly. The Holy Spirit draws the heart. Each person must choose whether to trust Him.

You can look to Jesus now

You do not have to wait until you understand every Bible teaching.

You do not have to repair your entire life first.

You do not have to become someone from another culture.

Come as you are, but come willing to be changed.

The Creator’s invitation is simple:

Look to Jesus.

Trust what He has done.

Receive life.

Think About It

  1. Why did some Israelites refuse to look even though they were dying?
  2. What does the serpent’s poison help us understand about sin?
  3. How did the bronze serpent point forward to Jesus?
  4. Has the misuse of the cross by religious institutions affected how you see Jesus?
  5. Are you looking more at your failures than at your Savior?
  6. What would trusting Jesus look like in your life today?

Try This During the Coming Week

Day 1

Read Numbers 21:4–9 ↗.

Write down what the people did, what the Creator provided, and what each person had to choose.

Day 2

Read 2 Kings 18:1–4 ↗.

Consider whether any object, symbol, person, or tradition has been given spiritual authority that belongs only to the Creator.

Day 3

Read John 3:14–17 ↗.

Write John 3:16 ↗ in your own words, using your name if that helps make the promise personal.

Day 4

Read Isaiah 53:4–6 ↗.

Write down what Jesus carried for you.

Day 5

Read 1 John 1:9 ↗ and Romans 8:1 ↗.

Confess a specific sin and thank Jesus for His promised forgiveness.

Day 6

Read Ephesians 2:8–10 ↗.

Make two lists: what Jesus does to save you and how your life can respond to His grace.

Day 7

Read Hebrews 12:1–3 ↗.

Identify one distraction or sin that keeps pulling your attention away from Jesus. Ask the Holy Spirit to help you lay it aside.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator, I admit that sin has wounded my life. I cannot remove its poison or save myself.

Jesus, I look to You.

Thank You for willingly carrying my sin to the cross. Thank You for entering human suffering and transforming an instrument of death into a sign of hope.

Forgive my sins. Remove my guilt and give me eternal life.

Help me separate who You truly are from the ways people have misused Your name. Heal the wounds caused by religious abuse and show me Your real character.

When shame tells me to hide, turn my eyes back toward You. When I fall, help me rise and return.

Holy Spirit, keep my heart connected to Jesus. Teach me to live as someone who has received new life.

I trust Your promise. Amen.

Remember This

The bronze serpent had no magical power. Healing came from the Creator when the dying person looked in faith.

Jesus said the lifted serpent pointed to Him on the cross.

Sin brings death, but Jesus carried our sin and offers eternal life to everyone who trusts Him.

The cross has been misused by harmful institutions, but those abuses do not define Jesus. At the cross, He willingly entered human suffering to rescue people from every nation.

Do not keep staring only at your wound, your past, or your shame.

Look to Jesus and live.
